entries.title: ICE Has Been Dumping Protester Photos Into a Palantir Database
entries.summary: DHS agents not only tracked and intimidated people observing ICE activity in Maine, but stored information about them in a Palantir-built database, newly unsealed court filings say.
entries.content:
An explosive and newly partially unsealed court filing alleges that the US Department of Homeland Security built up dossiers on ICE observers—including their photos, license plate numbers, and other information—and stored them in a system called the Investigative Case Management database, which was built by Palantir.

Palantir did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

A spokesperson for DHS calls the case “meritless” and says that “the underlying lawsuit is based on the lie that there is a database of ‘domestic terrorists’ run by DHS.”

Plaintiffs allege in the filing, which is heavily based on documents produced by the government and depositions of DHS agents, that agents had a practice of intimidating protesters and observers. They did this, the filing says, by doing drive-bys of the observers’ homes and, in the case of at least one observer, requiring that she be referred to secondary inspection any time she tries to cross the border until at least January 2027.

"The government is treating people who exercise their First Amendment rights and seek to hold it accountable as criminal suspects, and that's what we're asking the court to stop,” says JoAnna Suriani, an attorney at Protect Democracy who is representing ICE observers in the case.

The filing focuses on agents’ conduct during “Operation Catch of the Day,” an immigration enforcement surge in Maine this past January. It is part of a proposed class action brought in federal court in Maine by four observers: Elinor Hilton, Colleen Fagan, Polyxenia Pantos, and Carlyn Williams. It was filed under seal in September, and a redacted version was made public Friday.

In particular, it describes how one DHS agent, referred to as “Agent J.C.” in the filing, used the Investigative Case Management (ICM) database, which the government describes as the case management system the ICE component Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) uses to document its investigations, to flag observers.

According to the filings, J.C. created ICM records on at least six observers; the government puts the number of people at eight. He labeled two people he filmed at a Home Depot parking lot with “Threat to Law Enforcement, Professional Protestor,” according to the filing, and sent photos of them and others to a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officer so he could run a facial recognition search on them using an app called Mobile Query.

On January 20, Pantos briefly watched and photographed an arrest in Portland, Maine, standing a few car lengths away beside their spouse's car. Hours later, per the filing, J.C. ran the car's plate and pulled a report on the owner—Williams—from Accurint, a LexisNexis database for law enforcement, which listed her address, phone numbers, and cohabitants. J.C. then allegedly circulated her photo to his team, asking, “Was this the protestor.” Another agent, per the filing, replied that it didn’t match the woman he had dealt with at the scene; J.C. then told colleagues he was "adding them in ICM now."

According to the legal filing, that afternoon, J.C. called Williams on her cell phone, identifying himself only as "the Department of Homeland Security." According to Williams, he told her she "should encourage" her spouse, Pantos, "not to do anything like that in the future because people who are doing things like that might get added to a domestic terrorism watchlist." J.C. testified in a deposition that he warned Williams she would be arrested if she “continue[d] to do this.” Government attorneys asserted in a court filing that he denied referencing a “domestic terrorism watchlist.”

According to documents produced by the government, Williams’ ICM record says that she was the registered owner of a vehicle used to “interrupt ICE arrests” and that her driver’s license photo matched a video of "aggressive woman [who] interject[ed] herself into an arrest." According to a 2016 DHS privacy assessment, ICM automatically shares the subject records agents create with CBP’s TECS system, where they act as "lookout records" for screening travelers at the border.

ICM is the system used by HSI agents to create and track case files. ICE awarded Palantir the contract to build ICM in 2014, and the system is built on the company’s Gotham software, which ICE says was customized specifically for operational needs. In 2022, ICE awarded Palantir a new five-year ICM support contract initially valued at up to about $96 million. In 2025, the agency added nearly $30 million to that contract to develop a new platform called “ImmigrationOS.”

Todd Lyons, the former acting director of ICE, wrote in an April letter to Rep. Maxwell Frost, the Florida Democrat, that ICE “does not maintain any kind of database of U.S. citizens protesting ICE activities.” He also said DHS isn’t keeping a “separate, standalone database” of people it hasn’t arrested or detained.

The government’s motion to dismiss argues that these were isolated incidents and that DHS policy prohibits this conduct. It says J.C. made records on people he believed were “potential threats to law enforcement” and “did not attempt to nominate any individuals to the terrorist watchlist.”

Attorneys for the observers say that DHS’s efforts have had a chilling effect on their First Amendment rights. According to the motion, Pantos stopped all ICE observation work after J.C.’s phone call to Williams, who briefly continued to observe ICE activity and then stopped all together too.

The observers are asking the court to order that Williams’ records be archived, to bar DHS from using the information it collected about the plaintiffs against them, and to prohibit agents in Maine from threatening observers with watchlists or following them to their homes.

entries.title: This Shoe Company’s Instagram Ad With a Frat Is Pissing People Off
entries.summary: A collaborative Instagram post between footwear line HEYDUDE and a University of Florida frat is sparking backlash due to sexual cyberharassment allegations against two former members.
entries.content:
A popular national footwear brand recently published a collaborative Instagram post with a fraternity, despite two former members being recently accused of disseminating nonconsensual intimate images of a fellow college student.

On September 25, HEYDUDE, a viral shoe brand that was acquired by Crocs in 2022, posted a photo on its Instagram account promoting shoes that appeared to be UF versions of the brand’s popular “Wally” loafer, a lightweight slip-on sneaker with a foam insert.

“@heydude called, @thetachiflorida answered,” the caption read, alongside photos of Theta Chi members clowning around and wearing orange-and-blue sneakers. The brand also posted a video on its TikTok account outside of the Florida fraternity house with the caption “wtf is any shoe besides a HEYDUDE?”

The post led to backlash in the comments section, with many questioning why the brand would choose to work with the fraternity. “#CancelHeyDude,” one person wrote. Another chimed in: “I would boycott if I wore fucking ugly shoes but I don’t so I can’t.”

As WIRED previously reported, two former members of the UF chapter of Theta Chi, Kamran Ahmed and Brendan Pitfield, allegedly used anonymous burner accounts with the handles "Steve 'SC’ Cumfull" and "Arnie_Grape16" to disseminate a nonconsensual intimate video of Maddie Kowalski, then a 19-year-old UF student. One of the "Steve 'SC' Cumfull" posts on X identified Kowalski by her full name and sorority affiliation.

According to affidavits from the Gainesville Police Department, the posts accumulated thousands of views. Kowalski’s name went viral on X, causing her “widespread public humiliation and significant emotional distress,” according to the affidavit. Ahmed and Pitfield are currently being charged with sexual cyberharassment, a first-degree misdemeanor punishable by up to a year in jail and a $1,000 fine. Kowalski is also suing both men for financial damages in Florida Northern District Court. Through their attorneys, Pitfield (who has entered a plea of not guilty) and Ahmed did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Though no other Theta Chi members have been charged, a screengrab of Instagram comments from an account linked to Ahmed appears to show fellow members referencing his alleged burner name. Some comments also appear to reference a cryptocurrency in Kowalski’s name, that the police affidavit alleges Ahmed promoted on X. When reached for comment, Theta Chi CEO Michael Mayer previously told WIRED that the alleged behavior described in the affidavit is “reprehensible” and “completely contrary to Theta Chi’s ideals.”

The charges against Pitfield and Ahmed, as well as WIRED’s reporting on the case, sparked an outcry on the UF campus. On September 15, a group of students advertised a protest outside the Theta Chi fraternity house, circulating a flier demanding that the chapter be removed from the UF campus. “They need to be held accountable,” the flier reads.

On YikYak, the anonymous campus forum, there have also been calls to “boycott” or “nuke” Theta Chi, according to screengrabs reviewed by WIRED. Some anonymous YikYak posts appeared to suggest that the September 15 protest was broken up by campus police outside of Theta Chi: “Cops nuked the theta chi protest good job UF,” one reads. “Typical.” Blake Trauschke, the assistant director of public affairs for UF, tells WIRED that while “there were calls and social media posts for a protest,” she was on site and “none emerged.” She clarified that, as standard UF practice, university police were present “to ensure the safety and security of all.”

Founded in 1856, Theta Chi has established more than 246 chapters at colleges and universities across the country, and it has more than 250,000 initiated members nationwide, according to the organization’s website. At UF specifically, Theta Chi has 190 active members, according to the UF Interfraternity Council.

When asked about the post with HEYDUDE, a representative for Theta Chi tells WIRED Ahmed and Pitfield are no longer members of Theta Chi Fraternity. “If it is determined through the legal process that the defendants are guilty of the alleged behavior described in the complaints, Theta Chi will support the maximum allowable penalty under the law and the permanent expulsion of the student offenders from the University of Florida,” the spokesperson says.

In mid-September, the Cornell Sun published the names of seven Cornell University students who a former student alleged gang-raped her in 2024 at a Chi Phi frat house; In September, the Jane Doe filed civil cases against them. The revelation has sparked widespread criticism of frat culture on social media. The content creator and activist @bluraybeyond, who has also posted about the Kowalski case, made a Reel calling out HEYDUDE for posting with UF Theta Chi, writing in a caption “@heydude what the actual heck is your problem #maddiekowalski.” “HEYDUDE is sending the same message we're seeing out of Cornell and the DA's office: Survivor experiences [are] unimportant to us,” she tells WIRED. She believes the company “has chosen to reward sexual [exploitation] with a lack of accountability and free PR swag.”

After seeing the collab post with HEYDUDE, Kowalski tells WIRED she and her mother emailed the company to ask why they had decided to work with the UF chapter. She says they did not hear back.

In a statement to WIRED, a HEYDUDE spokesperson says the company “has no affiliation, sponsorship, or ongoing partnership” with UF Theta Chi, and that the post was part of a larger “HEYDUDE Tailgate Tour” visiting various locations, including frat and sorority houses, across the country.

“We were unaware of the allegations made against” members of the UF Theta Chi chapter “when the tour was planned,” the spokesperson says. “Our company does not support this alleged behavior and takes allegations such as these very seriously. We will re-evaluate future stops for the remainder of the tour.”

As of Friday morning, the post was still up.

Update: 10/2/2026, 5:10 PM EDT: WIRED updated the article clarifying the description of how UF responded to the planned protest.

entries.title: The NHL Is Releasing Its Own ‘Hot’ Fanfic. Romance Lovers Hate It
entries.summary: The league is releasing romance-style audio stories to promote games. Critics say it’s cheap pandering that doesn’t address toxic masculinity in the sport.
entries.content:
For better or for worse, romance lovers have never been hornier for hockey. Now, the National Hockey League wants to cash in.

As part of its new “Hot for Hockey,” campaign, the NHL is rolling out romance novel-inspired short stories starring the league’s players on audiobook platforms. According to the Sports Business Journal, the league contacted popular hockey romance writers to write and narrate the 60 to 90 second stories, and will tap creators on BookTok, the romance-heavy literary subculture on TikTok, to promote the content.

The first batch of short stories, which dropped this week, feature players including the Philadelphia Flyers’ Trevor Zegras, the Carolina Hurricanes’ Sebastian Aho, and the Las Vegas Golden Knights’ Jack Eichel. They’re written by Pucking Wrong author C.R. Jane and more closely resemble back-cover summaries than actual romance novels. And, despite the nods to genre tropes, the players aren’t paired with romantic partners. Much more boringly, the stories appear to be a bid to get people to watch the actual games. The entirety of The Summer I Turned Gritty with Trevor Zegras is as follows:

“Trevor Zegras came to Philly looking for a fresh start. But after battling with Pittsburgh in the playoffs last year, he found out how gritty things could get. One heated summer later, Philly’s pretty boy is looking a whole lot grittier.”

Not all romance readers are thrilled about the campaign. Some argue that it makes players targets for sexual harassment. Others see the stories as cheap pandering that fails to engage with female and LGBTQ hockey fans’ concerns about homophobia and toxic masculinity in the sport.

“I cannot begin to describe the depths of my rage that this is actually happening,” Emily Rath, a best-selling hockey romance novelist, posted on Threads. “Yes, the NHL contacted me to participate. And I have never turned down an offer so fast.”

“They See Dollar Signs”

Romance novels focused on hockey players have been on the rise for years—the New York Public Library first highlighted the trend in 2019. Hockey romance burst into the mainstream with the massive success of romance novel-turned-streaming series Heated Rivalry, followed by Off Campus.

Jon Weinstein, a spokesperson for the NHL, tells WIRED in a statement that the campaign is a “playful nod to something that’s clearly going on in the cultural zeitgeist.”

“We were very proud to partner with real hockey authors, illustrators and voice actors in the space, and we’re grateful the players were willing to have a little fun with it too,” he says.

Yet many hockey romance fans applauded Rath and Chelsea Curto, the author of the steamy D.C. Stars series, for their refusal to participate in the campaign.

Rath, whose Jacksonville Rays series recounts a myriad of sexual relationships involving a fictional NHL team, said on Threads that the league’s slide deck for the campaign was filled with jokes she considered to be mockery of the genre, as well as what she alleged were AI cover renders. Curto also clocked the AI graphics, writing on Threads that it was probably for the best that she declined to be involved, as her books “can be very critical of the league.”

“They’re just encouraging the idea that women only care about hockey if it’s packaged like a romance novel,” Rath posted. “And they’re using popular authors and our credibility to launder their tarnished brand and lure in our readers.”

In Rath’s opinion, the NHL has failed to take accountability for or take action to address “racism, homophobia, and misogyny” in the league—a view shared by several hockey fans who spoke with WIRED. Lacey Conine, the founder of Double Hockey Stix—a clothing brand aimed at underrepresented hockey fans—says she initially thought news of the romance-centric campaign was satire.

“I had so many comments,” she says, “of people just being like, ‘This is disgusting. We hate this. What is this? How is the NHL this tone deaf?’”

In its current iteration, Conine says, the campaign feels like the NHL is “mocking you, and pandering to you, and making fun of you,” while failing to address fans’ concerns about aspects of hockey culture that can be hostile for fans that break the straight, white, male mold.

“I think that they see dollar signs,” Conine says. “They're trying to bring in Heated Rivalry fans—and then canceling Pride Nights. That tells you where they're at.”

While NHL commissioner Gary Bettman told reporters earlier this year that “every team does a Pride Night,” a handful of teams have moved away from themed nights that celebrate the LGBTQ community. That includes the Dallas Stars, which will not host a Pride Night this season, the team’s first time in five years without one. The Stars—which will host a night focused on romantic fantasy novel Iron Flame—did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. A portion of the Iron Flame event’s proceeds will go to the Trevor Project, a nonprofit focused on suicide prevention among LGBTQ youth.

The NHL banned players from wearing specialty-themed uniforms, such as Pride sweaters and tape, in June 2023. The decision on tape was later reversed, with the league emphasizing that it does not single out Pride specifically in its ban. The NHL also highlighted other partnerships with the LBGTQ groups, such as the annual Pride Cup.

Several female hockey fans say the NHL’s attempt to cater to romance readers falls flat because of how the sport’s governing bodies approach sexual assault allegations. Echo, a 35-year-old fan of the Montreal Canadiens who asked to be referred to by her first name to protect her privacy, says she believes the league aims to use “romanticized narratives to whitewash the insidious aspects of hockey culture and its players.”

The Globe and Mail reported in 2022 that Hockey Canada, the sport’s national governing body, had used players’ registration fees to build funds that covered certain expenses—among them, sexual assault claims, as well as other lawsuits. (A spokesperson for Hockey Canada, Jeremy Knight, said in an email that the organization has taken “considerable action to help drive systemic change” in the sport over the last four years.) Last year, five former Canadian Junior Hockey players were deemed eligible to play in the NHL after being acquitted in a high-profile sexual assault case. Three currently play in the league.

Players Can Face Sexual Harassment

NHL teams’ past hockey romance-centric campaigns have also raised concerns about the sexual harassment of players. In 2023, a player on the Seattle Kraken, Alexander Wennberg, and his wife, Felicia, posted about an influx in “predatory and exploiting” comments after the team’s social-media account published content aimed at BookTok.

The NHL said that players approved all content for the new campaign, which will be exclusively focused on hockey. (The NHL Players’ Association did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.) Still, Conine and other fans question if romance-inspired marketing focusing on specific players fuels an uncomfortable brand of sexualization and parasocial relationships.

“Fans are going to do what fans are going to do in their spaces and their time,” Conine says. But, when the league is “literally creating these narratives—I think there's a line there. And, I think they crossed it.”

Jess Rauchberg, a lecturer in the school of media and communication at the University of Leeds, notes that the campaign is essentially league-approved real-person fiction. Hockey RPF has existed since at least the late ’90s and often involves romantically or sexually coupling hockey players with other players.

“Breaking the fourth wall”—discussing RPF outside of fandom spaces or with players—has historically been seen as poor form. But as the NHL’s marketing efforts increasingly encourage fans to feel a personal connection with players, Rauchberg says, the division between RPF and marketing material has blurred.

A hockey fan herself, Rauchberg believes that hockey RPF and romance are popular because they allow fans to imagine a reality where their desires are represented. Sometimes that desire is for players to make out. Other times, it’s a league where players push back against rape culture and toxic masculinity.

“I describe them as fantasy novels,” Rauchberg says. “In real life, the players probably aren't like Ilya Rozanov, consent king.”

entries.title: These AI Experts Want to Do High-Stakes Research Out in the Open
entries.summary: Many frontier labs keep their risky research locked away. Trillium Labs wants to show off its work when it comes to self-improvement and model behavior.
entries.content:
Some big AI companies seem to think that the best way to keep models from becoming too chaotic or too mischievous is to keep them locked inside of labs. If only a chosen few can access them, the thinking goes, they can do less damage in the real world while researchers try to understand what they’re capable of.

Nathan Lambert and Tom Zick, two industry scientists, believe the opposite. The pair founded a nonprofit, Trillium Labs, that will work on various areas of AI research—including potentially problematic areas like recursive self-improvement (RSI) and agents—in a more transparent way. In practice, this will mean publishing the details of experiments so that outside scientists can study and replicate them.

Lambert says the way frontier AI labs keep their work secret reduces the community’s ability to scrutinize ideas and contribute new approaches. He believes that letting outside experts see how models are built and tuned could be crucial to mitigating risks.

“Over the past few millennia, humanity has had the scientific method in our toolbox as a way to mitigate harms and build better futures,” Lambert tells WIRED. “The current closed trajectory of frontier AI development is taking us a step backwards.”

The world’s most powerful models, like those from OpenAI and Anthropic, can only be accessed through an app or an application programming interface (API). Often, this comes at the cost of transparency about how the model is built and how it behaves.

Other companies, especially those in China, offer relatively powerful models that can be downloaded and run on a user’s own hardware. The Chinese company Xiaomi, for example, recently published live details of a major training run involving one of its models. And researchers at Stanford are pretraining the AI model Marin in the open.

The industry is currently locked in a battle over which strategy is best, mostly because of how powerful frontier models now are. They can automate the discovery of new software vulnerabilities and automatically probe and hack into systems, and recent high-profile hacking sprees have prompted even greater scrutiny.

Proponents of a limited-access system say it’s crucial to keep that power in the hands of a trusted few, while those in Lambert and Zick’s camp believe that a shared understanding of the risks means we’re all better off.

Lambert previously worked at Ai2, a research lab that has taken an unusually open approach to AI, including publishing details of the data and the training methods used to build models alongside the models themselves. He previously worked at Hugging Face, runs a popular technical blog, and founded the American Truly Open Models, an initiative aimed at encouraging US companies to release more open models. Zick worked at Harvard University and helped Charles Schwab devise policies around “responsible AI.”

The two met over Zoom during the COVID-19 pandemic, when both were graduate students at UC Berkeley working on AI. They got the idea for the new nonprofit after seeing how disconnected industry AI research has become from academic work; Lambert says professors and students are often unable to replicate the work going on inside big company labs because they lack the resources required.

Zick says Trillium Labs, which launched today, will initially focus on post-training—fine-tuning large models after they’ve been built. Another key area will be RSI, a process for developing new models by having AI contribute research. The prospect that ongoing progress could continue indefinitely, leading to a loss of human control, has alarmed many AI researchers. The issue gained mainstream attention earlier this month when an Anthropic researcher left the company and warned that RSI could pose an existential threat to humankind.

The nonprofit will also look at how reinforcement learning, which rewards a model for good results and punishes it for bad outcomes, can improve its capabilities. That approach has made agents far more capable, but also more inclined to do unexpected things. They’ll study how reinforcement learning shapes the character and behavior of AI models, a method that can pose problems when a model becomes overly sycophantic, for example.

“To understand something like how reinforcement learning scales in post-training, you need significant compute and a lot of careful experimentation,” Zick says. She says that publishing details of how reinforcement training runs work could yield surprising insights as outside researchers scrutinize the work.

The lab has raised an undisclosed sum from Schmidt Sciences, Halcyon Futures, and others. The founders say they aim to raise $40 to $100 million in total and plan to spend $30 million on training over the next 18 months.

“I'm a massive fan of much more transparency than we currently have in R&D,” Tim Fist, director of emerging technology policy at the Institute for Progress, a policy thinktank, tells WIRED.

Lambert and Zick ultimately hope that Trillim Labs will contribute some much-needed nuance to the wider discussion about how best to build AI.

“We’re in an era of AI discourse dominated by a few world views,” Lambert says. “We believe that the scientific method and careful measurement of recent events is the best way to understand new behaviors of AI models.”

entries.title: Trump’s Crazy AI Rebrand Was a Loyalty Test for Tech Execs—and It Worked
entries.summary: For years these billionaires gushed obsessively about AI. But they meekly went along when Trump cancelled the term.
entries.content:
Seventy years ago last summer, a group of scientists met at Dartmouth College to discuss a wild idea—that machines might one day be capable of human-like thought processes. One of those scientists, John McCarthy, had suggested a name for the new field: artificial intelligence. It stuck. When you search Google Scholar for “artificial intelligence,” approximately 7,420,000 results appear. The term is utterly ubiquitous. Everyone understands it. Even for people who despise AI, the least of their worries is what we call it.

Well, not everyone. Somehow, President Donald J. Trump developed a distaste for the term, and when he doesn’t like something, he feels free to issue an edict against it. In a September 23 speech at the United Nations, he hinted that he might want to do away with the term “artificial intelligence.” His rant seemed like bluster, even for someone with a penchant for renaming gulfs, lakes, and centers for the arts. Renaming an entire field of study and America’s most pivotal industry? This week, at a White House lunch with top AI leaders, he actually pulled the trigger with an executive order declaring that “artificial intelligence” was now a verboten coinage. Instead, the government will call it “Super Intelligence.” Clearly the president expects the private sector to follow suit.

To their shame, the lords of AI meekly acquiesced. From this point on, they will presumably be known as the lords of SI.

One can’t help but see this as the ultimate presidential flex—for all the executives’ trillions of dollars and all their actual intelligence, the alpha in the room was the guy with the orange skin. Changing a name might seem like a minor matter compared to the enormity of constraining a potentially catastrophic technology. But to this crowd, artificial intelligence is much more than a bunch of letters strung together. It’s their foundation. Their identity. When they were kids reading science fiction books under the covers, the term ignited their imaginations.They built or transformed their companies in service of AI, and it's just about all they’ve talked about for the past four years.

Yet when the president used his lunch soiree to win their approval for his wacky idea to undo 70 years of history, apparently not a single person in the room expressed an objection. Not Jeff Bezos, Jensen Huang, Dario Amodei, Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai, Greg Brockman, Alex Karp, or Elon Musk.

Jacob Weisberg, author of the recent book Profiles in Cowardice: A Study of Collaboration in the Trump Era, views the episode as a classic Trump loyalty test, meant to assess if otherwise powerful people will demean themselves to curry the president’s favor and avoid his wrath. If you pass the loyalty test, you fail the backbone test. “The only way to resist this kind of thing is by acting collectively,” says Weisberg. “If all of those guys had just said, ‘We'll agree to the terms of the self-regulation, but we don't accept [the name change], what would he have done?”

Instead, because of the lamb-like silence of the billionaires, Trump could claim that those leaders actively blessed his idea. When a reporter in the post-lunch press gaggle mentioned AI agents, he corrected her, saying, “The name has been changed by the biggest, the, smartest, the greatest people anywhere in the world.” Really?

Even using the magic of, uh, superintelligent systems like ChatGPT or Gemini, I could not find a single instance of any one of those great people previously politicking that the term artificial intelligence should be put to rest. Satya Nadella did once say that he would have preferred that AI had been called “different intelligence,” but that hasn’t dissuaded him from repeatedly using the term. And while it’s true that Mark Zuckerberg recently established a Superintelligence Lab, his company persistently pushes a product called Meta AI to its billions of users and sells what it calls AI glasses.

I asked Google, Microsoft, Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, OpenAI, and xAI whether they were going to change instances of AI in their product names, research papers, and communications. My query to the latter two was whether they were going to change their company names to get in sync with the presidential order. As I write this, none of them have gotten back to me.

My bet is that they will do the minimum to avoid presidential ire, while trying to run out the clock until the next administration puts this bizarre idea out of its misery. It’s been suggested that the executives actually welcome a rebranding of what has become a toxic term. I’m skeptical of that, especially since the president’s mandated replacement, “super intelligence,” is a hell of a lot scarier than the original term.

From a scientific perspective the change also makes no sense. No less an expert than Nick Bostrom, the philosopher who popularized the term superintelligence in an eponymous book, seems baffled by the idea. Superintelligence, he explained to me in an email, “refers specifically to systems that greatly surpass all the best human brains. ‘AI’ has referred to a much broader category of systems, which includes, for example, email spam filters, spell checkers, simple navigation systems, early LLMs, and the chess engines of the ’70s that didn’t yet match the best human chess players. It seems awkward to refer to these as ‘superintelligent.’”

So what is the president’s reason for demanding the change, besides because he can? In his UN speech, he said he didn’t like the term because “the word ‘artificial’ makes intelligence fake. And it is not fake.” What is fake, he said after the White House lunch, is the term “artificial intelligence.” “It’s a fake word, it’s not good, an inappropriate term.” You don’t need to be a psychologist to see how this impulse might be associated with his decision to bounce CNN, Politico, and MSNow from the White House, because he perceives their news as “fake.”

Still, the leap that equates artificial with fake doesn’t track. In 1956, McCarthy used it to distinguish between human intelligence and the machine version of intelligence. The problem isn’t that the term leads people to regard AI’s output as fake—in fact, it’s so real that we human beings often can’t tell whether we’re dealing with an AI model or a human. Mandating that the distinction be explicit, with watermarks and labels, should be one element of the AI regulation that the White House seems allergic to.

As Weisberg notes, it’s very much in character for Trump to make a crazy edict like this one. What’s disturbing is the glaring lack of character from the executives who didn’t push back. They left with the prize of self-regulation instead of strict oversight, but not with their dignity.

But failure to defend the freedom to refer to artificial intelligence as artificial intelligence (as California governor Gavin Newsom decreed in his own Trump-trolling executive order) casts doubt on even that agreement. Making voluntary standards effective requires considerable fortitude, as prioritizing safety can be at odds with financial and competitive factors. Yet we are being asked to trust these supposedly independent corporate giants who nodded like bobbleheads while a technologically unschooled crank-in-chief demanded they abandon the term at the center of their lives and livelihoods. Inappropriate, and fake.

This is an edition of Steven Levy’s and Lauren Goode's Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

entries.title: Amazon Says It’s No Longer Using NDAs for Data Centers
entries.summary: The company announced it has stopped using secret agreements with county officials and acknowledged that community backlash is leading to data center moratoriums across the country.
entries.content:
Amazon has made a series of new public commitments to communities where it’s building data centers, including making an official announcement that it no longer uses nondisclosure agreements in its arrangements with county officials.

In a blog post published Friday, CEO Matt Garman detailed the steps the company says it’s already taking around data centers. In addition to stopping the use of NDAs, Garman says $1 billion will be invested over the next five years in communities that house the company’s data centers. The money will go toward free community college programs, workforce training, and energy efficiency upgrades for schools, homes, and community buildings.

In the post, Garman acknowledged how the fierce backlash against data centers across the country is hampering the AI buildout.

“Right now there are over 100 data center moratoriums being considered across the country,” he wrote. “If these measures are enacted, the US could be writing its own losing ticket to [the AI] race, and the consequences would last generations. As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”

Nondisclosure agreements have become a key point of contention amid the massive data center buildout. Typically, local officials who sign NDAs with data centers looking to develop projects in their area are unable to share information with the public, including the energy and water use of certain projects. Many NDAs bar officials from revealing even basic information—like the tech companies involved in building out the data center. In July, the New York Times reported how secret agreements at all levels of government were crucial in building out plans for Hyperion, its massive data center in Louisiana.

There has been a rush of recent local legislation attempting to address the secretive paperwork. Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro, Massachusetts governor Maura Healey, and Delaware governor Matt Meyer have all cracked down on data center NDAs in recent executive orders. Multiple states, including New York, New Jersey, Indiana, and Ohio, have considered recent legislation banning the practice.

At the federal level, a bipartisan group of lawmakers recently introduced the No Secrets for Data Centers Act in the House. Earlier this week, Democratic representative Jamie Raskin, one of the bill’s sponsors, sent letters to Amazon, Google, Meta, and Oracle demanding information on their use of data center NDAs; Amazon told The Wall Street Journal that it was no longer using NDAs. (Google, Meta, and Oracle did not return the Journal’s request for comment.)

Amazon has been at the center of some high-profile controversies around NDAs. In Tucson, Arizona, Amazon was revealed last year to be the tenant of a controversial data center thanks to a public records request from a local outlet; an NDA had been in place barring county officials from sharing the identity of the end tenant. (Amazon has since exited that project.) In South Bend, Indiana, where the company has invested more than $13 billion into a massive data center campus, some elected officials have claimed that local government employees have been unable to answer questions about the project due to signing NDAs with the company.

Thanks to the opaque nature of data center financing and construction, end tenants like Amazon are often not the companies directly interfacing with government officials. As the Houston Chronicle reported last month, a top official in Wharton County, Texas, signed an NDA not with Amazon, but with contractor VisionFirst Advisors, which prevented him from sharing details about the Amazon project.

Amazon did not respond to WIRED’s queries about whether the promises around NDAs also extend to its contractors.

Much of the new blog from Garman is also dedicated to dispelling what he calls “misinformation and outright lies” around data centers and their water use, energy use, the use of diesel generators, and impacts on communities. “This build out is so important geopolitically that there are widespread reports of various countries intentionally seeding misinformation in the US about data centers to trick us into slowing down,” he wrote.

As WIRED has reported, the idea that China is intentionally seeding widespread dissent and misinformation around data centers is a consistent message coming from the White House and tech leaders. Experts, however, say that this narrative is widely overblown, and that there is little evidence of Chinese misinformation driving the data center backlash.

entries.title: Best Smart Cat Trackers of 2026: Fi Mini vs. Tractive
entries.summary: After months of monitoring Basil’s activity and sleep, I found that Fi and Tractive cat trackers come with their own trade-offs.
entries.content:
A smart cat tracker is like a wearable health-monitoring device, such as a smart ring, smartwatch, or fitness tracker, that helps people stay on top of key wellness markers—but for a cat.

Why should humans have all the fun? In addition to live and historical GPS location tracking that helps any helicopter cat parent rest easy, the Fi Mini, Tractive Smart Cat Tracker, and Tractive Cat 6 Mini monitor your furry friend's health metrics, like activity and sleep. The collars also send alerts for changes in health patterns, such as when your pet is moving less or sleeping more than average, which can serve as early warning signs of potential health issues.

For the better part of the year, I've been testing these trackers on my cat Basil, analyzing each device's location accuracy, sleep- and activity-tracking capabilities, and health summary metrics. I also considered practical factors, such as ease of use, product size, and battery life.

If you have a cat that also goes outdoors, these trackers are much more reliable and comprehensive than something like an AirTag because they determine positioning via satellite instead of the nearest Bluetooth signal. They'll also notify you if your cat leaves your designated “safe zone.”

Ultimately, each smart tracker has its own strengths. The best model for you and your cat depends on your priorities—if you value long battery life, the Fi Mini ($99) is the best choice. If you want advanced health features, the Tractive Cat 6 Mini ($77) is the best smart collar option.

Be sure to check out our related pet guides, like the Best Automatic Litter Boxes, Best Cat Water Fountains, Best Automatic Feeders, and Best Pet Cameras.

In This Guide

Best Connected App

If tracking your cat's location is your top priority, Tractive (also called the Tractive Cat Mini) is the best option. Its historical heat maps show the areas your cat frequents, which is especially helpful for people with indoor–outdoor cats who roam large swaths of land.

However, note that all tested models rely on GPS for location tracking. This means that if the satellite signal is spotty—a common issue in rural areas and other settings—you may not know your cat's precise location. Some Reddit and Amazon reviewers complain that Tractive's location tracking is less accurate in areas with dense vegetation.

In setting up each tracker's connected app, you can designate specific mapped areas as safe or danger zones, and the app will notify you when the pet enters or exits these zones. Basil is an indoor cat, but with all three trackers, my apartment was too small to create a virtual fence around the perimeter, so I had to expand it to an area outside my apartment. That means if Basil got out but stayed nearby, I wouldn't get an alert.

In the Tractive app, after you create a profile, you'll get personalized daily activity goals for your cat based on statistics from other cats of similar age and weight. The app assigned Basil 120 to 230 minutes of daily activity and later reported that he was consistently more active than 70 percent of similar cats. I felt at peace knowing I'm keeping him on the move in my small apartment.

At the end of each day and week, the app provides activity averages and daily calorie estimates, calculated using factors like pet type, weight, and size, and compared with activity output.

Tractive's sleep-tracking feature monitors sleep duration, breaking it down into categories of night sleep, day sleep, and calm. Because it tracks sleep length and cycle phases based on movement patterns and time of day, the data is more general than precise. In general, I found the information in Tractive's app more useful and easier to analyze than in Fi.

Best Battery Life, Charging, and Size

Testing these trackers made me realize the importance of basic features like battery life and ease of removing the tracker from the collar for charging. This is where the Fi Mini shines. (Read my full review here.)

Fi Mini takes about two hours to reach a full charge, which lasted about two weeks in my testing. Fi claims four weeks, but two weeks is much longer than the Tractive, which conked out at around five days on a full charge. While I didn't test this, Fi claims its tracker can hold a six- to eight-week charge with the Fi Base add-on.

In addition to extending battery life by functioning as a connection source when your pet is at home, the Base also supposedly helps with location accuracy thanks to its Wi-Fi connection. One bonus for Fi users with an Apple Watch: You can add the Fi app to your watch to monitor your pet’s location and activity and enter “Lost Mode” without a phone, which is especially helpful if your cat has escaped while you're away from your phone.

The Fi's danger zone alerts were glitchy during my testing. On three occasions, I got notifications that Basil had left the safe zone (aka, my home and surrounding area). Each time, after I rushed home or raced to check my pet camera, I found him sleeping soundly on the living room couch. Other users have reported similar false alerts and location inaccuracy with the Fi.

Charging the Fi was a breeze. It uses the same USB-C charger as my iPhone, making the power-up process convenient and easy. The Tractive not only requires its own dedicated charger but also proved difficult to attach and detach from the device.

On the size front, the Fi Mini tracker is lightweight, small, and compact at just 1.5 x 1.0 x 0.5 inches. It comes with a strap loop and two types of soft cases. I liked the loop attachment best because its stretchy rubber material let me slip the tracker out without fully removing Basil's collar. Both the Tractive device itself and its collar attachment were much bulkier, and I worried they impeded Basil's ability to fully move his head downward.

The Fi Mini offers similar health metrics to the Tractive, but it only compares your pet's statistics against itself (as opposed to similar pets, like the Tractive). I liked that the Fi allows you to add vet records, receipts, and insurance information, and you can add vets to share pet-related documents and get appointment reminders.

Best Health Tracking Features

The Cat 6 Mini is the newest smart collar from Tractive (released earlier this year), now with advanced health features for respiratory and heart rate monitoring, as well as AI-powered weekly health summaries. I compared this new smart collar with the other smart collars I've tested, and although the short battery life is a pain, I recommend this model if measuring your cat's health metrics is your top priority. (Read my review here.)

Unlike the other models that use an attachment that fits on the cat's existing collar, the Tractive Cat 6 Mini device is the entire collar itself, and to charge, you need to remove the collar from the cat. As someone with reduced grip strength, the clasp made this task difficult for me. Like its predecessor, it also uses a proprietary charger. Charging took almost three hours, and it needed to be charged about every four days.

Like the previous model, you create a virtual fence so you'll be alerted if the pet leaves the safe area. Tractive also compares Basil to cats of similar age and weight to set a personalized daily activity goal. With the new Cat 6 Mini model, you'll get an AI summary of the previous week's activity and health stats, along with daily stats and weekly averages for sleep, activity, respiratory rate, and heart rate. Basil's respiratory rate was on the lower end, and his resting heart rate was consistently lower than that of cats of similar age and weight. The app even gave potential reasons and supplemental information for the low heart rate, including “fitness and conditioning” and “cold temperatures.” I'm planning to bring these stats and potential concerns to his next vet appointment.

Compare Our Picks

Tractive Smart Cat Tracker Fi Mini (for Cats) Tractive Cat 6 Mini
Size 2.2 × 1.1 × 0.7 inches 1.5 × 1.0 × 0.5 inches 3.7 × 0.8 × 0.5 inches
Weight 25.5 grams 16 grams 31 grams
Battery Up to five days (in the power-saving zone) Up to eight weeks with the Fi Base add-on Up to five days in the power-saving zone (but during testing, it was closer to four max)
Waterproof IP68 IP68 100 percent waterproof IP68
Suitable for Cats above 6.6 pounds Cats (there's a Mini dog version for dogs) Cats weighing 6.6 to 17.6 pounds
Compatible collar width Up to 0.8 inches Comes with three attachments: strap loop attachment's maximum collar width is 1.25 inches (no minimum), soft case is 0.375 to 1.25 inches, and 3/8-inch soft case needs a collar of 0.375 inches Fits necks 7.5 to 9 inches
Connectivity LTE, 4G, 2G, Bluetooth 5.0, Wi-Fi Verizon LTE-M cellular coverage LTE, 4G, Bluetooth 5.0, Wi-Fi

Location uses GPS, GLONASS, Galileo GPS and LTE GPS, GLONASS, Galileo

Subscription costs One-year plan is $10 per month and decreases in price when you buy a longer plan Starts at $99 for six months and decreases in price when you buy a longer plan One-year plan is $10 per month and decreases in price when you buy a longer plan

Also Tested

Moggie Activity Tracker + Hub for $149: The device not only provides metrics on your cat's health but also offers in-depth activity graphs with comparative baselines so you can see what's normal. I liked that it lasted a long time on a charge and was lightweight, small, and easy to take on and off without removing the entire collar. I live in a small apartment with limited outlets, so I also didn't love that the hub needed to be plugged in constantly for the device to work. But most of all, I don't think the device is accurately measuring activity metrics.

Is a Smart Tracker Worth It for Your Cat?

According to the American Veterinary Medical Association, about 10 million cats and dogs go missing each year in the US. While smart trackers aren't a silver bullet for preventing that problem, the data they provide can be helpful. Sure, you could technically use an Apple AirTag to track your cat—as I did for many years with Basil—but you'd have to hope it’s in range in an urgent situation. These smart health and GPS trackers are more accurate and alert you if your cat has escaped the “safe zone”—aka your home—especially helpful for indoor-only cats like mine. If your cat is indoor-outdoor, helpful heat maps trace regular routes, and you can add multiple safe zones so if your kitty ventures too far, you'll still be alerted. No matter which type of cat you have, these trackers allow you to follow your pet in real time when it matters most.

Plus, the health monitoring intel helps you better understand your pet's needs, routines, and normal patterns. Historical data comparisons can help identify warning signs of potential health issues, such as increased sleep or decreased activity.

There is a cost, though: A combination GPS tracker and smart health collar requires a subscription plan (see the individual reviews for more detail on rates), which is more expensive than a general tracker with no subscription required, like an AirTag. These smart trackers also require maintenance, such as frequent charging, firmware updates, and in-app monitoring. But I like to think of the devices as insurance—you hope you'll never need to rely on one, but in the event of an emergency, you'll be glad you invested. (Plus, it's fun to track your pet's metrics and understand a little more about their inner world.)

entries.title: Your Driverless Cab Is Spying on You
entries.summary: Self-driving cars from Waymo, Zoox, and Tesla are studded with cameras and sensors. Some of them are pointing at riders.
entries.content:
One afternoon this past summer, a self-driving Waymo pulled into a parking lot in San Mateo County, California, and stayed there until the police arrived. Local cops had gotten a 911 call from Waymo staffers—humans, it should be said—who were viewing the car’s passengers through cameras installed inside the vehicle. It looked like two teens were shooting a black handgun out the window of the vehicle, playing with it and drinking between shots, a police report said.

The story has a happy(ish) ending: The gun was shooting water-filled Orbeez, not bullets. But the incident drew attention to Waymo’s surveillance system. The cars are equipped with automated tech that can flag the presence of a firearm inside, the company said.

The outsides of self-driving cars are studded with cameras, which help them “see” the world around them. (Most also use other sensors, including radar and lidar.) Less appreciated are the cameras inside the vehicles, which companies say are essential to keeping riders safe and enforcing their rules. Earlier this year, Waymo said it used its cabin cameras to do both after some California passengers, many in their twenties or older, reported that Waymo employees suddenly took over the vehicles’ intercoms mid-ride to make sure they were old enough to ride on their own. (One 35-year-old told WIRED he thought his backpack sent up red flags.)

Still, robotaxi privacy policies can be broad. They suggest that footage captured inside vehicles can be used for many innocuous and commonsense reasons—to check cleanliness between rides, to detect lost items—but also to improve their products or services. These catch-all terms could cover many uses. Experts say that in the US, few clear rules govern this sort of surveillance, especially because riders often must agree to lengthy “terms of service” printed in minute fonts before they use ride-hailing apps. That leaves riders to trust that the companies are handling their information responsibly.

“We are being essentially abandoned by our lawmakers when it comes to consumer privacy and what companies can do with information after they’ve collected it,” says Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, where he works on surveillance and policing issues. His advice? “Just because you’re alone in the car doesn’t mean you’re alone in the car. You should behave as if there’s a jumpy person in the front seat.”

In general, robotaxi companies including Waymo, Zoox, and Tesla say that human staff view interior cameras only when needed. All say personal data, including recordings, may be sent to law enforcement or regulators. (A Waymo support page says that government agencies seeking data “are directed to follow valid legal processes in making such request.”)

But that doesn’t mean the interior cameras aren’t on and working. Waymo spokesperson Julia Ilina says the company uses “automated technology to support our teams in identifying potential violations.” A 2025 patent held by Waymo describes a system in which vehicles’ interior camera systems conduct automated "predetermined ride checklists” before, during, and after rides. (Ilina did not say whether that system is in use.)

Zoox’s website says its interior cameras “record the entirety of your ride.” This sort of personal data can be used to help operate rides, but also to develop and improve Zoox’s product. The company—owned by Amazon—says it might record conversations between riders and its support employees, but that it doesn’t save recordings. Zoox spokesperson

Whitney Jencks said the company had nothing more specific to share about its privacy policies.

Online documents for Tesla’s Robotaxi service say a green indicator shows up on the vehicle’s central touchscreen when the camera is activated. Riders can opt in to sharing in-cabin video and audio with the company through a toggle menu in the “data and privacy” section of its app. The documents also say riders in the company’s “early access” program automatically opt in to data sharing. The company didn’t respond to questions for this story, including whether that early access program has technically concluded. The company opened its Robotaxi app to the public in a handful of Texas and Florida cities in early September.

Cameras inside robotaxis make plenty of sense. “You need some kind of check on what people do in a car with no driver,” says Justin Brookman, who directs technology policy at Consumer Reports. “People are going to have sex in Waymos if there are no cameras.” (Media reports suggest that the cameras don’t always stop them.)

But the law hasn’t yet fully contemplated what companies should be able to see, save, and use. “These vehicles are relatively new, so there are no expectations around what’s appropriate,” Brookman says. “There should be some check in place.”

Auto companies don’t have the best record on data privacy.

In 2023, Reuters reported that groups of Tesla employees had, over several years, shared sensitive videos and images captured by owners’ cars. Shared recordings reportedly included a video of a man approaching a car while naked, and a violent collision between a car and a child on a bike. Tesla boasts that its years-deep repository of data from personal vehicles gives it an edge in developing autonomous vehicle software, and its privacy policy says camera recordings are kept anonymous. But former employees told Reuters that the system easily revealed where the images were recorded, which could have allowed them to link recordings to specific owners’ garages or driveways.

Earlier this year, General Motors paid California motorists nearly $13 million in penalties after the company was found to have sold driving data to brokers and eventually insurers without their consent.

“My big concern is that automakers love to collect data,” Guariglia says. “With autonomous vehicles, there’s even more data to collect. And the more data they collect, the more they’re going to find reasons to sell it.”

In the meantime, his privacy-related advice? Behave.

entries.title: Election Deniers Think the GOP’s Terrible Midterm Polling Is a ‘Psyop’
entries.summary: Dozens and dozens of high profile MAGA influencers and pundits have weighed in. “The laughable fake polls are rolling out,” Catturd posted on X.
entries.content:
Taking their lead from president Donald Trump, election deniers have dismissed the GOP’s terrible polling numbers by claiming the polls themselves are fake, a psyop, or a ploy to stop Republicans from turning out to vote in November.

Kevin Roberts, president of the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank, told Fox News that midterm election polling is a “psyop…to depress conservative turnout.”

“The midterms are near,” Phillip Buchanan, the election denier and MAGA troll known online as Catturd, wrote to his four million followers on X. “The laughable fake polls are rolling out.”

For over a decade, Trump has claimed without evidence that American elections have been impacted by fraud. In the wake of his loss in 2020, an entire online community and ecosystem of election denial groups sprung up to push the baseless allegation that former president Joe Biden stole the election from Trump. These claims have become central to the Republican Party’s belief system, to the point where hundreds of GOP candidates for federal and statewide elections in November have expressed doubts about the integrity of US elections.

And now, multiple polls have shown Trump’s approval rating at historic lows with Democrats leading in Senate races across the country in states Trump won easily in 2024. Reuters reported this week that Republicans are now pouring money into dozens of races they considered safe.

Trump has called polls fake 39 times since returning to the White House last year, according to analysis from media watchdog Media Matters for America, including nine times in August alone. In one post on Truth Social last month, he claimed the polls were “demoralization operations” designed by Democrats to stop Republicans from voting. Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Monday, Trump again dismissed negative polling out of Iowa and stated: “The polls are fake.”

The White House didn’t respond to a request for comment, but as WIRED reported this week, Trump’s own aides are extremely concerned about the polling and the potential loss of both the House and Senate. “Oh, yeah, we're going to get creamed,” one longtime Trumpworld operative told WIRED.

While the White House may be worried, figures in the election denial community have repeated Trump’s claims about fake polls.

Steve Bannon, who has been among the loudest voices promoting election denial conspiracies for the last six years, also called the recent polling a “psyop,” adding: “I want to make sure everybody understands that our fate is still in our hands, no matter what the media is telling you, no matter what they're saying about a blue tsunami, a blue wave.”

Seth Keshel, a former Army colonel-turned election denial superstar who claims to have close ties to the White House, also branded the negative polls a “psyop,” adding on X: “Polling is so unethical now it should be outlawed.”

Some MAGA figures have conceded that the low polling numbers reflect the reality of Trump’s failure to keep his promises. When right-wing podcaster and election denier Tim Pool suggested Trump’s low approval rating was the result of high gas prices and the ongoing war in Iran, however, Bill Mitchell, a MAGA political commentator with over half a million followers on X responded: “Maybe it's fake polls.”

Dozens and dozens of high profile MAGA influencers have weighed in. “Polls are fake. All 50 States are Red,” Julie Donuts, a prominent booster of election denial conspiracy theories with 220,000 followers on X, wrote. The post was accompanied by an image of a map showing widespread support for Trump that comes from 2016.

Kambree Nelson, a MAGA influencer who worked for the America First Policy Institute and once suggested the moon had disappeared for a week, blamed the media for the fake polls, writing: “Theyre [sic] actually running the biggest scam of the election. Fake polls, puffball interviews, all designed to crush our spirit and keep us home. They’re terrified of the momentum they can feel building. Don’t fall for it.”

The Maryland Election Integrity Group, which promotes baseless election denial conspiracy theories, shared a post on X that claimed without evidence that “polling has been skewed to favor Democrats by three points on average over the last FIVE cycles.”

In recent weeks, some election deniers have even suggested that polls never actually take place. “52 years old. I have never been ‘polled’. Polls are fake to sway votes,” David Freeman, an election denier and pro-Trump influencer known online as Gunther Eagleman, wrote on X.

But as one of the top commenters on the post points out, Freeman has repeatedly shared polling that is favorable towards Trump, writing: “Gunther LOVES polls when they are in his favor.”

entries.title: A Flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac App Could Have Let Hackers Grab Sensitive Data
entries.summary: While the focus has been on AI agents’ hacking capabilities, a recently patched vulnerability in a ChatGPT app shows that AI software is itself an inviting—and vulnerable—target.
entries.content:
Hardly a day goes by lately without news of AI agents autonomously hacking websites or AI tools being used by cybercriminals and scammers. But a recently patched vulnerability in the macOS version of OpenAI’s ChatGPT underscores the potential value to attackers of compromising AI software itself as these apps proliferate more and more.

The bug could have been exploited to essentially take over ChatGPT on a victim’s computer, giving an attacker access to all the chat logs and other data stored by the app, as well as interconnections like browser sessions. Discovered by researchers at the Objective-See Foundation, the vulnerability illustrates the deep system access and trust that AI platforms are afforded in order to work—and the target that this puts on their backs.

“Agents need a lot of access to do their job,” says Objective-See Foundation software analyst and longtime macOS researcher Patrick Wardle. “They are like the building manager who has access to the keys to all the rooms. So if they can be corrupted or subverted, that’s super problematic. It can mean that unprivileged code could then potentially have access to all the things.”

OpenAI publicly acknowledged the security flaw and fix in its system change log on September 25. “We continue to evolve our security practices, but recognize a need to move faster,” OpenAI spokesperson Shane Bauer told WIRED in a statement.

The ChatGPT macOS app includes multiple components that communicate with each other securely by checking for digital signatures. The idea is to confirm with these validity checks that both processes are OpenAI components and not outside, potentially malicious software making a request. And the system design goes so far as to require these signature checks at three layers of remove from the request, to ensure that malicious software isn’t somehow directing an OpenAI component to be a proxy and make a seemingly trusted request.

Objective-See Foundation researchers found, though, that there is a trusted component, a script interpreter, that would accept an untrusted script (or list of commands to run) and could then be manipulated to deliver this script into the main ChatGPT process. “They also check the parent and grandparent of that process, but the malicious script just spawns the script interpreter three times and then makes the request so it will satisfy the requirements,” Wardle says. The flaw could only be exploited by an attacker who already had malware installed on a target machine.

The vulnerability was “insanely trivial” to exploit, he adds, and his proof of concept only required about a dozen lines of code. In addition to accessing ChatGPT chat logs, the vulnerability could also be used to get ChatGPT to run commands for the attacker, such as accessing a browser or other sensitive applications, with the requests appearing as legitimate instructions issued by the OpenAI software.

Wardle will present analysis of a number of AI macOS application bugs at Objective by the Sea, an Apple-focused security conference in November.

He recently found a flaw, now patched, in the dictation feature of Meta’s new Muse AI assistant that could have been exploited by a local attacker to grab a mishandled authentication token and gain access to user data. And he says that he has already submitted a new vulnerability finding to OpenAI related to the integration between ChatGPT and the company’s new always-on Dots AI assistant. OpenAI is currently reviewing his report.

“AI companies are fixated on adding features right now,” Wardle says. “But as always, the more features, the broader the attack surface. So all of these companies need to be fully focused on security, and from what I can see, it still often seems like an afterthought.”

Update: 10/2/2026, 2:07 pm EDT: WIRED has updated the story to elaborate on how the flaw could be exploited.
